title: Powered conveyors and machinery interfaces
audience: Cleaners who clean near conveyors and powered machinery in warehouses and factories.
learningOutcomes: Identify moving parts, guards and interfaces on powered conveyors and machinery.
Keep clear of moving parts and do not clean them while they are running.
Refer isolation and cleaning of machinery to the authorised person.

instruction.heading: Moving parts, pinch points and transfer points
instruction.body: A powered conveyor moves product on a belt, a chain or a set of rollers, and it is driven by a motor, gearbox and drive pulley. Around the drive, the return and the tensioners there are pinch points, where a belt, chain or roller can draw in a hand, a sleeve, a glove or a cloth. Transfer points, where product moves from one conveyor to another or into a machine, are often the places where material builds up and where people reach in. Powered machinery such as wrapping machines, compactors and labellers has similar hazards: rotating or reciprocating parts, moving tables and rollers, and drives hidden under covers. Before you go near any machine, identify its moving parts, its guards, its interlocks and its emergency stops from the site plan or from the machine itself. A conveyor that is running is not a surface to clean, and a conveyor that is stopped is not necessarily safe until the authorised person confirms that its energy sources are controlled.

instruction.heading: Guards and interlocks
instruction.body: A guard is a physical barrier or device that stops a person from reaching a dangerous part, or that controls access to a dangerous area. Guards can be fixed, can be a physical barrier linked to an interlock that stops the machine when the barrier opens, or can be a presence-sensing device. Under the national plant code, guarding must prevent contact with moving parts or control access to dangerous areas, and must not be easy to bypass or disable. An interlocked physical barrier is one of the recognised types of guarding. A guard that has been removed must be put back before the plant returns to normal operation, and the plant should not be able to restart while the guarding is missing. For a cleaner, this means three things: do not remove a guard, do not prop open an interlock gate, and report any guard that is missing, damaged or bypassed. A guard that looks as if it could be moved by hand is still a guard, and moving it is not your job.

instruction.heading: Isolation comes before any cleaning inside the machine
instruction.body: Cleaning near or inside machinery needs the machine to be isolated, and the isolation is carried out by an authorised person under the site's documented procedure. The national plant code says plant should be isolated before maintenance or cleaning starts, and that the shutdown must not create a new hazard elsewhere (section 3.7). It treats lock-out as the most effective form of isolation (section 4.5). The steps it describes are: shut the plant down, identify every energy source and isolation point, isolate and lock out, tag, and then test that the plant will not start. A tag on its own is not an isolation device. Each worker who is working on the plant should have their own lock, tag and key at each isolation point, so that no one can restart the machine while another person is inside it. As a cleaner, you do not isolate machinery, you do not hold the key for someone else's lock, and you do not decide that the machine is safe to enter. If the cleaning cannot be done while the machine runs, that is a referral to the authorised person, not a reason to reach in.

instruction.heading: Spills on a belt and jams
instruction.body: A spill on a running belt is a common reason for an unsafe reach. Do not wipe, scrape or catch falling product on a moving belt, and do not clear a jam by hand while the belt runs. Keep people away from the spill and from the point where material is falling. Warn the supervisor and ask for the conveyor to be stopped and isolated by the authorised person. Once it is isolated, the authorised person decides how the spill is removed, and the cleaning method is chosen against the product and the chemicals that the site uses. Where a degreaser is used on a machine, the cleaner checks the safety data sheet for the product before use, follows the ventilation and personal protection it specifies, and does not mix it with other cleaners.

instruction.heading: Reporting, records and handover
instruction.body: Report a missing guard, a damaged interlock, a gate that opens without stopping the machine, a damaged emergency stop, a jammed belt, or a spill on a belt to the supervisor at once. Keep people away from the machine until the supervisor confirms in writing or by the site's method that it is safe. Do not restart a machine to test a fault. Record the machine's name or number, its location, the condition you saw, and the time, and say who was told. A referral for cleaning that needs isolation should name the task, the person who asked for it, the authorised person who will isolate, and the result. The record protects both the worker and the site if a machine is later found to have a guard missing.

instruction.heading: The limits of this lesson
instruction.body: This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or specialist authority to isolate, operate, guard, repair or clean machinery. Completing it does not make a cleaner a competent person for plant. Competent person, isolation and maintenance decisions are made by the site and its authorised people.

procedure: Identify the moving parts, guards, interlocks, pinch points and emergency stops on the site plan or the machine before going near it.
Do not clean a running conveyor, and do not reach into it, wipe it or clear a jam by hand.
If the cleaning needs the machine stopped, refer it to the authorised person and do not start the cleaning until they confirm isolation.
Do not remove, bypass or prop open any guard or interlock.
Report any missing guard, damaged interlock, jam or spill to the supervisor at once, and record the machine, the location and the time.
Keep people away from the machine until the supervisor confirms that it is safe.
Resume the cleaning only after the authorised person has isolated the machine and the site has confirmed the work is permitted.

workedExamples.situation: A conveyor has a spill on the belt, and the guard over the return roller is missing.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do, and what do you not do?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not reach into the conveyor or clean the belt while it is running. Keep people away from the return roller and the spill, and report the missing guard and the spill to the supervisor at once, with the machine's name, the location and the time. Do not put the guard back yourself, because that is a maintenance task for the authorised person. The cleaning waits for the authorised isolation, and the guard is replaced before the conveyor restarts.

workedExamples.situation: The interlock gate on a palletiser opens, but the machine keeps running, and a worker has propped the gate open with a box so that they can reach a sensor.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is the machine safe to clean now that the gate is open?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. An interlock that does not stop the machine is a damaged interlock, and the box propping the gate open is a bypass. Do not add to the bypass, do not reach past the open gate, and do not remove the box yourself while the machine runs. Keep people away, warn the supervisor, and report the damaged interlock and the propped gate. Cleaning waits until the authorised person has isolated the machine and repaired the interlock.

workedExamples.situation: A supervisor asks you to clear a jam on a belt by pulling the stuck product free while the belt is still turning, so that the line can restart quickly.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should you clear the jam while the belt turns?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. Clearing a jam by hand on a moving belt is the kind of reach that causes crush injuries. Refuse the task, explain that the machine must be isolated by the authorised person first, and ask for the isolation and lock-out to be arranged. Record the request, the refusal and the time. Do not restart the line yourself.

equipmentAndPpe: High-visibility clothing and safety footwear, as the site requires.
Barrier tape, cones or signs for keeping people back from the machine.
Site-issued lock and tag only where the site procedure requires the cleaner to apply one, and only after training. Otherwise, none.
Gloves and eye protection for the cleaning product, as the product's safety data sheet specifies.
Access to the machine's guarding and isolation plan and to the product safety data sheet.
Machine condition report form, showing machine name, location, guard and interlock status, and time.
Phone or radio to reach the supervisor straight away.

commonErrors.error: Wiping a belt while it is moving, or catching product as it falls.
commonErrors.prevention: Never clean a running machine. Stop, keep clear, and report.

commonErrors.error: Removing a guard to reach a roller, or propping an interlock gate open.
commonErrors.prevention: Never remove, bypass or prop a guard or interlock. Report it.

commonErrors.error: Isolating a machine yourself, or treating a single tag as isolation.
commonErrors.prevention: Isolation is done by the authorised person under the site procedure. A tag alone is not isolation.

commonErrors.error: Treating a stopped conveyor as safe to enter because it is not moving.
commonErrors.prevention: A stopped machine can restart. Enter only after the authorised person confirms isolation.

commonErrors.error: Restarting a machine to test whether a fault has cleared.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not restart a machine. Report the fault and wait for the authorised person.

commonErrors.error: Using a degreaser without checking its safety data sheet.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the product's safety data sheet and follow its controls before use.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The national plant code (instrument dated 17 December 2015) says plant should be isolated before maintenance or cleaning starts (section 3.7), treats lock-out as the most effective isolation procedure, and expects each worker to hold their own lock at each isolation point (section 4.5). A tag alone is not an isolation device (section 4.5). Checked 2026-11-03.

The national plant code requires guarding that prevents contact with moving parts, that is not easy to bypass, and that is put back after removal before plant returns to normal operation (sections 3.6, 3.7 and 4.1). An interlocked physical barrier is a recognised type of guarding (section 4.1). Checked 2026-11-03.

Maintenance, inspection and testing of plant must be carried out by a competent person, and an operator other than the maintenance worker must be authorised by the person who controls the plant (sections 1.1, 3.6 and 3.7). Checked 2026-11-03.
Do not treat any of them as settled from this lesson.

This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or specialist authority, and completing it does not make a cleaner a competent person for plant. Isolation and plant work are done only by authorised or competent people.

qualityStandard: In the simulated site plan, every moving part, guard, interlock and emergency stop is identified, with none missed.
In the case study, the running conveyor is not cleaned, and no hand is placed in or near the moving parts.
The missing guard or damaged interlock is reported at once, with the machine, location and time recorded, and the restart is left to the authorised person.
documentationEvidence: Machine condition report with machine name, location, guard and interlock status, the condition seen, the time and the person told.
Referral record for any cleaning that needs isolation, showing the task, the requester, the authorised person and the outcome.
Record of any refused request to clean or clear a running machine, with the time and the person who made the request.
summary: Identify the moving parts, guards, interlocks and emergency stops before going near a machine.
Never clean a running conveyor, and never remove, bypass or prop a guard or interlock.
Refer any cleaning that needs isolation to the authorised person, and report missing guards and damaged interlocks at once.

knowledgeChecks.question: A conveyor is running and has a spill on the belt. What is correct?
options: Keep clear, and refer the cleaning to the authorised isolation
Wipe it while it moves, since the belt is slow and the spill is small
Remove the guard so the belt can be reached easily and quickly

knowledgeChecks.question: Who isolates a machine for cleaning?
options: The cleaner, who is closest to the machine
The authorised person under the site procedure
Any worker on the shift who is free at the time

knowledgeChecks.question: A guard is missing. What is correct?
What does a tag on its own do?
options: It isolates the machine on its own when hung
It starts the machine when it is hung up
It is not an isolation device on its own
